airliner.text: How does a modern jet engine push a huge airliner across the sky? Look inside the cutaway: a giant spinning front fan splits incoming air into two completely different paths around a compact burning core. Let's step through the engine and discover where most of the forward push really comes from.

Start at the intake. The spinning giant orange front fan grabs an enormous river of air and splits it into two paths: in this design, eight parts sweep around the outside through the wide cool bypass duct, while just one part enters the inner metal core.

Now pause and compare the two streams leaving the back: the wide cool bypass river around the outside, and the compact blazing exhaust inside the inner core. Before you move on, predict which one produces most of this airliner's forward push.

It is the cool air! Eighty percent of a modern airliner's forward push comes from the cool bypass stream pushed by the giant front fan, and only twenty percent from the hot core jet. Gently pushing a huge amount of air uses far less fuel and makes far less noise than blasting a narrow fiery stream.

So what powers that giant front fan? Inside the core, tight spinning steel compressor blades squeeze the incoming air thirty times tighter. Then fuel sprays into the glowing burner ring, where it burns steadily and expands outward with huge force.

That rushing hot gas spins the brass rear turbine at the back. In this design, the turbine extracts eighty percent of the core's energy and sends it straight forward along the solid center drive shaft to keep the compressor and the giant front fan spinning continuously.

Changing the bypass ratio trades quiet fuel savings for raw jet speed. An eight-to-one airliner puts eighty percent of its push into the cool bypass stream, while a one-to-one fighter puts sixty-five percent into its blazing hot core exhaust. fighter.text: How does a compact fighter jet engine punch through the sky at blazing speed? Look inside this one-to-one cutaway: a slim bypass duct wraps tightly around a roaring burning core. Let's step through the engine to see how that tight split changes where the forward push comes from.

Start at the intake. The spinning giant orange front fan grabs an enormous river of air and splits it into two paths: in this design, one part sweeps around the outside through the slim cool bypass duct, while just one part enters the inner metal core.

Now pause and compare the two streams leaving the back: the slim cool bypass stream around the outside, and the roaring blazing exhaust inside the inner core. Before you move on, predict which one produces most of this compact fighter's forward push.

It is the hot core jet! In this compact one-to-one fighter engine, the slim bypass duct only gives thirty-five percent of the push, while sixty-five percent comes from the blazing hot core jet. That narrow, super-fast exhaust favors raw speed, though it burns fuel fast and roars loudly.

So what powers that giant front fan? Inside the core, tight spinning steel compressor blades squeeze the incoming air thirty times tighter. Then fuel sprays into the glowing burner ring, where it burns steadily and expands outward with huge force.

That rushing hot gas spins the brass rear turbine at the back. In this design, the turbine extracts fifty-five percent of the core's energy and sends it straight forward along the solid center drive shaft to keep the compressor and the giant front fan spinning continuously.

Changing the bypass ratio trades quiet fuel savings for raw jet speed. An eight-to-one airliner puts eighty percent of its push into the cool bypass stream, while a one-to-one fighter puts sixty-five percent into its blazing hot core exhaust.
